habitat: African wild dogs roam the savannas, grasslands, and open woodlands of sub-Saharan Africa. They are found in scattered populations from South Africa to Tanzania, with significant strongholds in Botswana, Zimbabwe, and parts of East Africa. They prefer areas with low prey density and avoid dense forests and extreme desert environments. Their range has contracted dramatically, and they now occupy less than 7% of their historic range.
diet: African wild dogs are specialized pack hunters, primarily preying on medium-sized antelopes such as impala, gazelle, and kudu. They hunt cooperatively, with the pack working together to pursue prey over long distances at speeds of 50-60 kilometers per hour. Their hunting success rate is an extraordinary 70-80% — the highest of any African predator, far exceeding lions at 25-30%. Prey is typically torn apart and consumed rapidly to avoid theft by larger predators.
behavior: African wild dogs live in tightly bonded packs of 2-30 individuals, usually dominated by a monogamous breeding pair. The pack is characterized by remarkable cooperation: puppies are fed by all pack members through regurgitation, and sick or injured adults are cared for by the group. Unlike most social mammals, female African wild dogs disperse from their natal pack while males typically remain. They communicate through touch, body posture, and a distinctive repertoire of birdlike chirps and twitters — they cannot bark or howl.
facts: Each African wild dog has a unique coat pattern of black, white, brown, and yellow patches, like a fingerprint. They have only four toes per foot (most dogs have five), an adaptation for speed. Their large, rounded ears serve two purposes: exceptional hearing for locating prey and thermoregulation in the hot African climate. Fewer than 6,600 African wild dogs remain in the wild, making them one of Africa's most endangered carnivores. They are also known as painted wolves or Cape hunting dogs.
naming: Names for African wild dog-themed pets might reflect their pack loyalty, unique coat patterns, or African origin. Consider names like Painted, Patches, Speckle, Swift, Delta, Kalahari, Savanna, Okavango, Mosi (first in Swahili), Rafiki (friend), Mwezi (moon), Jua (sun), or Zuberi (strong).
